nameStory: The White-rumped Sandpiper gets its name from the distinctive white patch above its tail that becomes clearly visible when the bird takes flight. This bright white "rump" acts like a natural name tag, helping birdwatchers distinguish it from the many other small, similar-looking sandpipers that all tend to blend together on the beach.
description: The White-rumped Sandpiper is a small, brownish shorebird about the size of a sparrow that visits New England's coastlines during migration. Like other "peeps" (the nickname for small sandpipers), it has a slender build with long legs for wading and a straight, dark bill perfect for probing wet sand. Its overall coloring is a mottled brown and white that helps it blend in perfectly with wet sand and pebbles. When standing still among its cousins, it can be nearly impossible to pick out, but the moment it flies, that telltale white rump gives it away.

idTips.label: White rump patch
idTips.description: A bright white patch above the tail that flashes conspicuously in flight, looking like a small white flag against the brown back

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Slightly larger than a Least Sandpiper but smaller than a Dunlin, with a more elongated body shape that looks stretched out compared to other peeps

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Straight, dark bill that's medium-length for a peep - not as tiny as a Least Sandpiper's but not as long and curved as a Dunlin's

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Dark grayish-black legs that contrast with the lighter body, unlike the yellowish legs of Least Sandpipers

idTips.label: Wing extension
idTips.description: When standing, the wingtips extend noticeably beyond the tail, giving it a more streamlined appearance than other small sandpipers

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Often feeds in slightly deeper water than other peeps, methodically probing the sand with a sewing machine-like rhythm

habitat: White-rumped Sandpipers prefer mudflats, salt marshes, and sandy beaches along New England's coast, especially areas with scattered pools and channels where they can probe for small crustaceans and marine worms. They're often found feeding alongside other small sandpipers on exposed tidal flats during low tide. Unlike some sandpipers that stick to the surf line, White-rumped Sandpipers venture into slightly deeper water and more varied coastal habitats.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs in late May and early June, when birds show their cleanest breeding plumage with crisp streaking on the breast and back. Look for them in mixed flocks with other migrating sandpipers.
seasonality.summer: Most birds have passed through to Arctic breeding grounds, though occasional stragglers or non-breeding individuals may linger along the coast in worn, faded plumage.
seasonality.fall: Best viewing season from late July through September, when both adults and juveniles pass through in large numbers. Fall birds show more muted, grayish-brown plumage.
seasonality.winter: Very rare in winter, as these long-distance migrants continue south to Central and South America. Any winter sightings would be exceptional.

funFact: White-rumped Sandpipers are among the longest-distance migrants in the bird world, flying over 9,000 miles from their Arctic breeding grounds all the way to Argentina - that's like flying from New York to Tokyo, but twice a year!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other "peeps" like Semipalmated and Least Sandpipers when on the ground. Remember the white rump rule: if you can't see the white rump, wait for it to fly - that bright white patch is your guaranteed ID ticket. Memory trick: "When in doubt, flush it out" - the white rump will solve the mystery instantly.
contextualKnowledge: The term "peeps" comes from the high-pitched calls these small sandpipers make, and birdwatchers use this nickname affectionately for the group of tiny, brown, look-alike sandpipers that can drive even experienced birders to distraction. White-rumped Sandpipers are considered one of the more reliable peeps to identify once you know the key field marks.
compareHints: Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast. Compared to the common Semipalmated and Least Sandpipers, White-rumped is slightly larger and longer-winged, with that diagnostic white rump patch that neither of the others possesses. The wing-tip extension beyond the tail is also more pronounced in White-rumped than in other small peeps.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
